opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more important points that sometimes gets lost when we compare architectures. In-context recall tasks, like needle-in-a-haystack or associative recall, where you're asked to retrieve an exact token or key-value pair that appeared somewhere earlier in the context, are almost by construction the ideal setting for a Transformer. Attention keeps the entire context explicitly in memory. The KV cache stores every token, so retrieval is essentially a lookup: you compute similarity between the query and all the keys and pull out the matching value. As long as everything fits in the context window, you have perfect, lossless memory of the past.

Recurrent models, linear attention variants, state space models, and our own work like Titans, are fundamentally different. They compress the past into a fixed-size state or memory. That's the whole point. It's what gives you linear complexity and the ability, in principle, to scale to very long or even unbounded sequences. But compression means you're going to lose some information. So if your benchmark measures exact retrieval of arbitrary details within a window that the Transformer can fully hold, you're testing the one thing that a lossless cache does perfectly and a compressive memory, by design, does not.

So it's a bit like comparing a system with a photographic but bounded memory against one that learns and abstracts. If the test is "repeat back token 3,000 verbatim," the photographic one wins. But that's not really what we want from intelligence, or even from most real tasks. Human memory doesn't work that way either. We forget, we prioritize what's surprising or important, and we generalize.

I'd also say there's a subtle issue with how the benchmarks are constructed. They're often designed within context lengths where attention is still feasible, so you never see the regime where the Transformer's quadratic cost or fixed window becomes the bottleneck. Once you go beyond that, to millions of tokens, or tasks where you need to integrate and reason over information rather than just copy it, the picture changes quite a bit. In some of our experiments, models with deep neural memory actually perform competitively or better on very long-context tasks like BABILong, precisely because they can keep learning what to store at test time.

So I don't think recall benchmarks are useless. They do reveal a real weakness of compressive models, and it's something we should work on, for example through better memory management, forgetting mechanisms, or hybrid designs that combine attention as short-term memory with a neural long-term memory. But if we treat recall as the main yardstick, we're implicitly defining "good memory" as "what attention does," and that biases the whole field toward Transformers.

r001.rationale: It calls in-context recall tasks “by construction the ideal setting for a Transformer” and explains that exact-retrieval benchmarks favor its lossless cache.

r002.rationale: It says attention keeps the entire context available and retrieval is a lookup over the keys to pull out the matching value.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that in-context recall is basically the task Transformers were built for. If you look at what attention actually does mechanistically, it's a lookup. You have a query, you compare it against every key in the context, and you retrieve the corresponding value. There's no compression, no forgetting. The entire history is sitting there in the KV cache, and the model can go back and pull out any token exactly. So when you design a benchmark that says, here's a key somewhere in a long sequence, now tell me the value associated with it, you're essentially asking, can you do attention? And of course Transformers can, because that's literally the operation.

For recurrent models or linear attention or state space models, the situation is very different. These models have a fixed-size memory. Everything they've seen has to be squeezed into a vector or a matrix of fixed dimension, and so you're forced to make decisions about what to keep and what to throw away. That's a compression problem. And compression is fundamentally lossy. So if the benchmark is "retrieve this exact needle," you're penalizing the model for the very thing that makes it efficient, which is that it doesn't store everything.

I think there's also a subtler point about why this became the standard comparison. It's easy to measure, it's clean, and there's a very clear winner, so it's a convenient story. But I'd argue it's a bit of a biased lens. A lot of what we care about in language modeling, in reasoning, is not exact retrieval of a random token. It's more like, what are the patterns, what's the structure, what generalizes. And on those kinds of tasks the gap between architectures is much smaller, and sometimes it flips. So when I see a paper that uses recall-heavy synthetic tasks to argue one architecture is strictly better, my reaction is, well, you picked the game where attention is the rule book. The more interesting question to me is how do we design memory that's smart about what it stores, rather than just asking whether it stores everything.

r001.rationale: The response says in-context recall is “basically the task Transformers were built for” and that recall benchmarks ask whether a model can perform attention.

r002.rationale: It explains that the full history remains in the KV cache and attention can retrieve a requested token exactly.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the task is very closely aligned with the mechanism of attention. In an in-context recall task, you put some information in the context, and later you ask the model to retrieve it. A Transformer keeps a representation of every token in its key-value cache, so when the query arrives, it can directly attend to the relevant information.

For a recurrent model with a fixed-size state, the problem is different. It has to compress the history into that state before it knows exactly what you’re going to ask. So if you fill the context with arbitrary key-value pairs and then ask for one particular value, you’re testing whether that compression preserved the exact association. The Transformer has access to a memory that grows with the context; the recurrent model has a fixed memory budget.

That doesn’t make recall an unimportant task. Exact retrieval matters. But it means we should be careful about treating performance on that task as a general ranking of architectures. It favors retaining everything and looking it up later, whereas other tasks may reward learning a compact representation of the history. Ideally, we’d evaluate both, and account for the memory and computation each architecture uses.

r001.rationale: The response says in-context recall is closely aligned with attention and favors architectures that retain the full context for later lookup, characterizing it as particularly suited to Transformers.

r002.rationale: It explains that a Transformer keeps each token’s representation in its key-value cache and can directly attend to the relevant information when queried.

sol-6.1.text:
I think in-context recall is almost designed around the strength of attention. A Transformer keeps the tokens in its context available, and when you ask a question, it can directly attend to the relevant information. So if the task is, “Here’s a key-value pair; later, tell me the value associated with that key,” attention has a very natural mechanism for solving it.

A recurrent model has a different constraint. It has to compress what it has seen into a state, and then retrieve the answer from that state. If you keep the state size fixed while increasing the amount of information it needs to remember, you’re creating a bottleneck that the Transformer doesn’t have in the same way. The Transformer’s memory grows with the context.

So these tasks are useful, but they measure a particular kind of memory: retaining and retrieving arbitrary information within a context. They don’t necessarily tell us which architecture is better at learning, generalizing, or remembering information over longer timescales. For a meaningful comparison, we should also account for how much memory and computation each architecture is allowed to use.

r001.rationale: The response says in-context recall is “almost designed around the strength of attention,” characterizing it as especially suited to Transformers.

r002.rationale: It explains that Transformers keep context tokens available and can directly attend to relevant information, making retrieval natural.
